nodes.name: pi (intro)
nodes.statement: Let $\pi$ be an infinite-dimensional irreducible unitary representation of ${\mathrm {GL}}_2 ({\mathbb {C}})$ with trivial central character (that is, a representation of $ {\mathrm {PGL}}_2 ({\mathbb {C}})$).

nodes.name: sigma (intro)
nodes.statement: Let $\sigma$ be an irreducible unitary representation of ${\mathrm {SL}}_2 ({\mathbb {C}})$.

nodes.name: Bessel function (intro)
nodes.statement: We attach to $\sigma$ the Bessel function $j_{\sigma, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi_1}$ on ${\mathrm {SL}}_2 ({\mathbb {C}})$ which is both left and right $(\psi_1, N)$-equivariant.

nodes.name: Bessel identity for the Waldspurger correspondence (sample form)
nodes.statement: Let $\pi $ be as above. There exists $\sigma$ as above such that for any $z \in {\mathbb {C}} \smallsetminus \{0\}$ we have \begin{align} i_{\hskip 0.5 pt \pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi_1} \begin{pmatrix} z / 4 & 1 \\ 1 & \end{pmatrix} = \frac {2 \epsilon (\pi, 1/2) \, \psi_1 \left ( 2 / z \right ) |z|} {L(\pi, 1/2)} j_{\sigma, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi_1} \begin{pmatrix} & - z\- \\ z \\ \end{pmatrix}, \end{align} in which $L (\pi, 1/2)$ and $\epsilon (\pi, 1/2)$ are the central values of the $L$-factor and the $\epsilon$-factor associated with $ \pi $.
conclusions: There exists $\sigma$ as above such that for any $z \in {\mathbb {C}} \smallsetminus \{0\}$ we have
nodes.statement_short: For each unitary $\pi$ of $\mathrm{PGL}_2(\mathbb{C})$ there is $\sigma$ of $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{C})$ whose Bessel function matches the relative Bessel function of $\pi$.
nodes.label: thm: main, intro

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.1 (sketch in introduction)
nodes.statement: The correspondence in Theorem \ref{thm: main, intro} is given by \begin{align*} \pi_{\mu, \hskip 0.5 pt m} \longrightarrow \sigma_{\frac 1 2 \mu, \hskip 0.5 pt \frac 1 2 m}, \hskip 10 pt \text{for } \mu \in i \hskip 0.5 pt {\mathbb {R}}, m \text{ even, or } \mu \in \big( 0, \tfrac 1 2\big) \hskip -1 pt , m = 0, \end{align*} reflecting the index correspondence $(\mu, m) \longrightarrow \big(\tfrac 1 2 \mu, \tfrac 1 2 m \big)$ between the Bessel functions on the two sides of \eqref{eq: main 1}. Here $\pi_{\mu, \hskip 0.5 pt m} $ and $\sigma_{\mu, \hskip 0.5 pt m} $ are the unitary principal series or complementary series of ${\mathrm {GL}}_2 ({\mathbb {C}})$ and ${\mathrm {SL}}_2 ({\mathbb {C}})$ parameterized by $(\mu, m)$ respectively (see \S \ref{sec: representations of G and S} for the definitions). To be precise, we have \begin{align*} j_{\pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi_1} \begin{pmatrix} & z \\ 1& \end{pmatrix} = & | z| \boldsymbol J_{ \mu,\hskip 0.5 pt m} \left ( - z \right ), \hskip 10 pt \pi = \pi_{\mu, \hskip 0.5 pt m}, \end{align*} \begin{align*} j_{\sigma, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi_1} \begin{pmatrix} & - z\- \\ z \\ \end{pmatrix} = (-1)^{\frac 1 2 m} \left| z \right|^{-2} \boldsymbol J_{\frac 1 2 \mu,\hskip 0.5 pt \frac 1 2 m} \left ( z^{-2} \right ), \hskip 10 pt \sigma = \sigma_{\frac 1 2 \mu, \hskip 0.5 pt \frac 1 2 m}, \end{align*} \footnote{It is preferred here to view $ j_{\pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi_1}$ as function on ${\mathrm {PGL}}_2 ({\mathbb {C}})$($= {\mathrm {PSL}}_2 ({\mathbb {C}})$).} and we shall prove in the sense of distributions that \begin{align*} i_{\hskip 0.5 pt \pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi_1} \begin{pmatrix} u & 1 \\ 1 & \end{pmatrix} = \frac 1 {L (\pi, 1/2)} \int_{ {\mathbb {C}} \smallsetminus \{0\}} j_{\pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi_1} \begin{pmatrix} & z \\ 1& \end{pmatrix} \psi_1 ( u z) \frac {d_1 z} {|z|^2 }, \end{align*} where $d_1 z$ denotes twice of the Lebesgue measure on ${\mathbb {C}}$. Moreover, note that $ \epsilon (\pi, 1/2) = i^{|m|} = (-1)^{\frac 1 2 m} $ if $ \pi = \pi_{\mu, \hskip 0.5 pt m} $. Thus the identity \eqref{0eq: Bessel identity} follows from the integral formula \eqref{eq: main 1}.
nodes.statement_short: Write both Bessel functions via $\boldsymbol J_{\mu,m}$, express $i_\pi$ as a Fourier transform of $j_\pi$, and apply the complex Weber-Hardy formula.

nodes.name: correspondence of parameters
nodes.statement: The correspondence in Theorem \ref{thm: main, intro} is given by \begin{align*} \pi_{\mu, \hskip 0.5 pt m} \longrightarrow \sigma_{\frac 1 2 \mu, \hskip 0.5 pt \frac 1 2 m}, \hskip 10 pt \text{for } \mu \in i \hskip 0.5 pt {\mathbb {R}}, m \text{ even, or } \mu \in \big( 0, \tfrac 1 2\big) \hskip -1 pt , m = 0, \end{align*} reflecting the index correspondence $(\mu, m) \longrightarrow \big(\tfrac 1 2 \mu, \tfrac 1 2 m \big)$ between the Bessel functions on the two sides of \eqref{eq: main 1}. Here $\pi_{\mu, \hskip 0.5 pt m} $ and $\sigma_{\mu, \hskip 0.5 pt m} $ are the unitary principal series or complementary series of ${\mathrm {GL}}_2 ({\mathbb {C}})$ and ${\mathrm {SL}}_2 ({\mathbb {C}})$ parameterized by $(\mu, m)$ respectively (see \S \ref{sec: representations of G and S} for the definitions).
nodes.statement_short: State the parameter correspondence $(\mu,m)\to(\mu/2,m/2)$.

nodes.name: explicit Bessel functions
nodes.statement: To be precise, we have \begin{align*} j_{\pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi_1} \begin{pmatrix} & z \\ 1& \end{pmatrix} = & | z| \boldsymbol J_{ \mu,\hskip 0.5 pt m} \left ( - z \right ), \hskip 10 pt \pi = \pi_{\mu, \hskip 0.5 pt m}, \end{align*} \begin{align*} j_{\sigma, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi_1} \begin{pmatrix} & - z\- \\ z \\ \end{pmatrix} = (-1)^{\frac 1 2 m} \left| z \right|^{-2} \boldsymbol J_{\frac 1 2 \mu,\hskip 0.5 pt \frac 1 2 m} \left ( z^{-2} \right ), \hskip 10 pt \sigma = \sigma_{\frac 1 2 \mu, \hskip 0.5 pt \frac 1 2 m}, \end{align*} \footnote{It is preferred here to view $ j_{\pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi_1}$ as function on ${\mathrm {PGL}}_2 ({\mathbb {C}})$($= {\mathrm {PSL}}_2 ({\mathbb {C}})$).} and we shall prove in the sense of distributions that \begin{align*} i_{\hskip 0.5 pt \pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi_1} \begin{pmatrix} u & 1 \\ 1 & \end{pmatrix} = \frac 1 {L (\pi, 1/2)} \int_{ {\mathbb {C}} \smallsetminus \{0\}} j_{\pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi_1} \begin{pmatrix} & z \\ 1& \end{pmatrix} \psi_1 ( u z) \frac {d_1 z} {|z|^2 }, \end{align*} where $d_1 z$ denotes twice of the Lebesgue measure on ${\mathbb {C}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Express $j_\pi$, $j_\sigma$ via $\boldsymbol J$ and $i_\pi$ as Fourier transform of $j_\pi$.

nodes.name: epsilon factor
nodes.statement: Moreover, note that $ \epsilon (\pi, 1/2) = i^{|m|} = (-1)^{\frac 1 2 m} $ if $ \pi = \pi_{\mu, \hskip 0.5 pt m} $.
nodes.statement_short: Evaluate the root number $\epsilon(\pi,1/2)=(-1)^{m/2}$.

nodes.name: conclude via (1.3)
nodes.statement: Thus the identity \eqref{0eq: Bessel identity} follows from the integral formula \eqref{eq: main 1}.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude from the complex Weber-Hardy formula.

nodes.name: Simplicity of the complex Waldspurger correspondence
nodes.statement: Admittedly, the Waldspurger correspondence over ${\mathbb {C}}$ is tremendously simpler than that over ${\mathbb {R}}$, because all the double covers of ${\mathrm {SL}}_2 ({\mathbb {C}})$ are isomorphic to the trivial product ${\mathrm {SL}}_2 ({\mathbb {C}}) \times \{\pm 1 \}$. Moreover, the representation theory of ${\mathrm {GL}}_2 ({\mathbb {C}})$ or ${\mathrm {SL}}_2 ({\mathbb {C}})$ is simpler as discrete series do not exist.

nodes.name: G and S
nodes.statement: Let $G={\mathrm {GL}}_2({\mathbb {C}})$ and $S={\mathrm {SL}}_2({\mathbb {C}})$.

nodes.name: B, A, Z
nodes.statement: Let $B $, $ A $ and $Z$ denote the Borel subgroup of upper triangular matrices, the diagonal subgroup and the center of $G$ respectively.

nodes.name: N and Weyl/torus elements
nodes.statement: Set \[ N=\left\{n(x)=\begin{pmatrix}1&x \\ &1 \end{pmatrix}:x\in {\mathbb {C}} \right\}, \] and \begin{align*} \varw = \begin{pmatrix} &-1 \\ 1& \end{pmatrix} &, \hskip 10 pt \varw_0=\begin{pmatrix} &1 \\ 1& \end{pmatrix}, \\ s(a) =\begin{pmatrix} a & \\ &a^{-1} \end{pmatrix} , \hskip 10 pt t(a)= &\begin{pmatrix} a& \\ &1 \end{pmatrix}, \hskip 10 pt z(c)=\begin{pmatrix} c& \\ &c \end{pmatrix}. \end{align*}
also_stated_at: Let \begin{align*} N = \left\{ \begin{pmatrix} 1 & z \\ & 1 \end{pmatrix} : z \in {\mathbb {C}} \right\}, \hskip 10 pt A = \left\{ \begin{pmatrix} a & \\ & b \end{pmatrix} : a, b \in {\mathbb {C}} \smallsetminus \{0\} \right\}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Unipotent subgroup $N$, Weyl elements $\varw,\varw_0$ and torus elements $s(a),t(a),z(c)$.

nodes.name: additive character psi_lambda
nodes.statement: For $\lambdaup \in {\mathbb {C}}$, let $\psi = \psi_{\lambdaup}$ be the additive character of ${\mathbb {C}}$ defined by $$ \psi_{\lambdaup} (z)=e ({\mathrm{Tr}} \hskip 0.5 pt (\lambdaup z)) = e (\lambdaup z + \overline {\lambdaup z}).$$

nodes.name: psi on N
nodes.statement: We also view $\psi$ as a character of $N$ by $\psi(n(z))=\psi(z)$.

nodes.name: measure dz
nodes.statement: Take $dz = d_{\lambdaup} z$ to be $2 \sqrt { \|\lambdaup\|}$ times of the Lebesgue measure on ${\mathbb {C}}$, which is self-dual with respect to $\psi$.

nodes.name: C^x
nodes.statement: Let ${\mathbb {C}}^{\times} = {\mathbb {C}} \smallsetminus \{0\}$.

nodes.name: multiplicative measure
nodes.statement: Set $d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt z=dz/\|z\| $.

nodes.name: psi-Fourier transform
nodes.statement: For $f\in L^1({\mathbb {C}} )$, we define the $\psi$-Fourier transform of $f$ as \begin{equation} \widehat f(u)= \int_{\mathbb {C}} f(z)\psi(uz)dz. \end{equation}
also_stated_at: Recall from \eqref{def: Fourier} that the Fourier transform with respect to the additive character $\psi (z) = \psi_{\lambdaup} (z) = e({\mathrm{Tr}}(\lambdaup z))$ is defined by \begin{align*} \widehat f (u) = \int_{ {\mathbb {C}}} f (z) \psi (uz) d z. \end{align*}

nodes.name: eq (2.1) Fourier transform
nodes.statement: \widehat f(u)= \int_{\mathbb {C}} f(z)\psi(uz)dz.
nodes.label: def: Fourier

nodes.name: self-duality of Fourier transform
nodes.statement: With our choice of measure $d z$, the Fourier transform is self-dual, namely, $\widehat {\widehat f } (u) = f (-u)$.
assumptions: With our choice of  measure $d z$
conclusions: the Fourier transform is self-dual, namely,  $\widehat  {\widehat f } (u) = f (-u)$

Langlands' classification for G
nodes.statement: According to Langlands' classification for $G$, any irreducible admissible representation of $G $ may be parametrized by $(\nu_1, \nu_2, l_1, l_2) \in {\mathbb {C}}^2 \times {\mathbb {Z}}^2$.
conclusions: any irreducible admissible representation of $G  $ may be parametrized by $(\nu_1, \nu_2, l_1, l_2) \in {\mathbb {C}}^2 \times {\mathbb {Z}}^2$

conclusions: $\mathrm{Ind}_B^G (\chiup_{\nu_1, \hskip 0.5 pt l_1}, \chiup_{\nu_2,\hskip 0.5 pt l_2}) $, defined by the unitary induction, has a unique irreducible quotient

nodes.name: principal series pi(chi1,chi2)
nodes.statement: We denote this quotient by $\pi (\chiup_{\nu_1, \hskip 0.5 pt l_1}, \chiup_{\nu_2,\hskip 0.5 pt l_2})$ according to \cite[\S 6]{J-L}.

nodes.name: principal series exhaust admissible duals
conclusions: these principal series $\pi (\chiup_{\nu_1, \hskip 0.5 pt l_1}, \chiup_{\nu_2,\hskip 0.5 pt l_2})$ exhaust all the irreducible admissible representations of $G$ up to infinitesimal equivalence

nodes.name: pi_{mu,m}
nodes.statement: For $\mu\in {\mathbb {C}}, m\in {\mathbb {Z}}$, we let $ \pi_{\mu,\hskip 0.5 pt m}$ denote the principal series of $G$ with parameter $\big(\mu, - \mu, \frac 1 2 m, - \frac 1 2 m \big)$ if $m$ is even or $ \big(\mu, - \mu, \frac 1 2 (m+1), - \frac 1 2 (m-1) \big) $ if $m$ is odd.

nodes.name: twists of pi_{mu,m} exhaust principal series
nodes.statement: Note that $\pi_{\mu, \hskip 0.5 pt m} \otimes \chiup_{\nu,\hskip 0.5 pt l} (\det)$ exhaust all the principal series of $G$ as above.
conclusions: $\pi_{\mu, \hskip 0.5 pt  m} \otimes \chiup_{\nu,\hskip 0.5 pt   l} (\det)$ exhaust all the principal series of $G$   as above

nodes.name: central character of pi_{mu,m}

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.1 (sketch)
nodes.statement: This lemma is a consequence of a much more general result of Jacquet and Shalika for ${\mathrm {GL}}_n $ over a local field in \cite[\S 4.4 Proposition 3]{Jacquet-Shalika:Exterior}. Specialized to the case of ${\mathrm {GL}}_2 ({\mathbb {C}})$, their result may be phrased as follows. There is a finite set $C$ of characters of ${\mathbb {C}}^{\times}$ with {\it positive} real part, namely, characters $\chiup $ with $|\chiup (z)| = \|z\|^{\rho}$ for $\rho > 0$, and for each $\chiup \in C$ a nonnegative integer $r_{\chiup}$ with the following property\footnote{For ${\mathrm {GL}}_2$, one should have $r_{\chiup} = 0$ or $1$.}: let $X$ be the set of finite functions of the form $\chiup (a) ( \log \|a\|)^{r}$, with $\chiup \in C$ and $r \leqslant r_{\chiup}$, then for any given $\varv \in H_{\infty}$ there are functions $\phi_{\xi}$ in the Schwartz space on ${\mathbb {C}} \times \mathrm{U}_2({\mathbb {C}})$ such that \begin{align*} W_{\varv} (t(a) k) = \sum_{ \xi\hskip 0.5 pt \in X } \phi_{\xi} (a, k) \xi (a). \end{align*} The rapid decay of $W_{\varv} (t(a))$ as $\|a\| \rightarrow \infty$ is already proven in \cite[\S 2.5]{Godement} (and also \cite[\S 6]{J-L}), in particular (68)-(72). However, we do not find any concrete statement in either \cite{J-L} or \cite{Godement} on the asymptotic of $W_{\varv} (t(a) )$ for $a$ small. Nevertheless, we may prove the asymptotic $W_{\varv} (t(a)) = O (\|a\|^{\rho}) $ as $\|a\| \rightarrow 0$ if we examine and estimate the integrals in (69) and (70) in \cite[\S 2.5]{Godement} more carefully; it is important here that $\pi$ is unitary so that either ${\mathrm{Re}\,} \mu = 0$ or $\mu \in \left ( 0, \frac 1 2 \right )$ (we may choose $0 < \rho < \frac 1 2 - {\mathrm{Re}\,} \mu$). It should be noted that only $\mathrm{U}_2 ({\mathbb {C}})$-finite vectors are treated in \cite[\S 6]{J-L} and \cite[\S 2.5]{Godement}.
nodes.statement_short: Specialize the Jacquet-Shalika asymptotic expansion; rapid decay from Godement, small-$a$ bound by re-estimating Godement's integrals using unitarity.

nodes.statement: Let $\varv\in H_\infty$, $f,g\in C^\infty({\mathbb {C}}^{\times})$. Assume that both $f(a)W_\varv(t(a))$ and $g(a)W_\varv(t(a))$ are in $L^1({\mathbb {C}}^{\times}, d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a)$. If \[ \int_{{\mathbb {C}}^{\times}} f(a)W_{\pi(n)\varv}(t(a))d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a=\int_{{\mathbb {C}}^{\times}} g(a)W_{\pi(n)\varv}(t(a))d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a \] for all $n\in N$, then $f(a)W_\varv(t(a))=g(a)W_\varv(t(a))$ for all $a\in {\mathbb {C}}^{\times}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.2
nodes.statement: The proof is literally the same as that of \cite[Lemma 2.1]{BaruchMao-Real}. We have \begin{align*} \int_{{\mathbb {C}}^{\times}} f(a)W_{\pi(n(x))\varv}(t(a))d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a = \hskip -1 pt \int_{{\mathbb {C}}^{\times}} f(a)W_{ \varv}(t(a) n(x))d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a = \hskip -1 pt \int_{{\mathbb {C}}^{\times}} f(a)W_{ \varv}(t(a) ) \psi (ax) d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a. \end{align*} Hence follows the integrability of the first integral for all $x \in {\mathbb {C}}$ and it is equal to the Fourier transform of the function $\|a\|\- f(a)W_{ \varv}(t(a) ) $. The identity in the lemma then yields the equality between the Fourier transform of $\|a\|\- f(a)W_{ \varv}(t(a) ) $ and that of $\|a\|\- g (a)W_{ \varv}(t(a) ) $. It follows that $f(a)W_\varv(t(a))=g(a)W_\varv(t(a))$ for all $a\in {\mathbb {C}}^{\times}$.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite as a Fourier transform of $\|a\|^{-1}fW_v(t(a))$ and use injectivity of the Fourier transform.

nodes.name: Crude bounds for the Bessel function J_{mu,m}
nodes.statement: Suppose that $|{\mathrm{Re}\,} \mu | < \rho$. We have \begin{equation*} \boldsymbol J_{ \mu,\hskip 0.5 pt m} \left ( z \right ) \lll \left\{\begin{split} & 1 / \left| z \right|^{2 \rho}, \hskip 11 pt \text{ if } |z| \leqslant 1, \\ & 1 /{\textstyle \sqrt {|z|}}, \hskip 10 pt \text{ if } |z| > 1, \end{split}\right. \end{equation*} with the implied constant depending only on $\mu$, $\rho$ and $m$. In particular, \begin{equation*} \boldsymbol J_{ \mu,\hskip 0.5 pt m} \left ( z \right ) \lll 1 / \left| z \right|^{2 \rho} + 1 / {\textstyle \sqrt {|z|}}. \end{equation*}
nodes.section: 4.1 The definition of $ \boldsymbol J_{\mu,\hskip 0.5 pt m} (z)$
nodes.statement_short: $\boldsymbol J_{\mu,m}(z)\ll |z|^{-2\rho}$ for $|z|\le1$ and $\ll |z|^{-1/2}$ for $|z|>1$.
conclusions: \begin{equation*} \boldsymbol J_{ \mu,\hskip 0.5 pt m} \left ( z \right ) \lll \left\{\begin{split} & 1 / \left| z \right|^{2 \rho}, \hskip 11 pt \text{ if } |z| \leqslant 1, \\ & 1 /{\textstyle \sqrt {|z|}}, \hskip 10 pt \text{ if } |z| > 1, \end{split}\right. \end{equation*} with the implied constant depending only on $\mu$, $\rho$ and $m$. In particular, \begin{equation*} \boldsymbol J_{ \mu,\hskip 0.5 pt m} \left ( z \right ) \lll 1 / \left| z \right|^{2 \rho} + 1 / {\textstyle \sqrt {|z|}}. \end{equation*}
nodes.label: 4lem: bounds for J

nodes.name: central character omega_pi
nodes.statement: The central character $\omega_{\pi} (z (c)) = c /|c|$ if $m$ is odd and $ \omega_{\pi} (z (c)) \equiv 1$ if $m$ is even.

nodes.name: Bessel function for GL_2(C)
nodes.statement: We define a function $j = j_{\pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi}$ supported on the open Bruhat cell $X = B \varw_0 B$ such that \begin{equation} j_{\pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi} ( t(a) \varw_0 ) = \left\{ \begin{split} & |\lambdaup a| \boldsymbol J_{ \mu,\hskip 0.5 pt m} \left ( - \lambdaup^2 a \right ), \hskip 42 pt \text {if } m \text{ is even},\\ & - i |\lambdaup| {\textstyle \sqrt { |a| a}} \boldsymbol J_{ \mu,\hskip 0.5 pt m} \left ( - \lambdaup^2 a \right ), \hskip 5 pt \text {if } m \text{ is odd}, \end{split} \right. \end{equation} \footnote{In \cite{Qi-Bessel}, as well as \cite{CPS}, the measure is not normalized by the factor $\sqrt {\|\lambdaup\|}$ and the choice of Weyl element is $\varw$ instead of $\varw_0$, so the Bessel functions in \cite[Proposition 18.5]{Qi-Bessel} are slightly different.} and that $j_{\pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi}$ is left and right $ (\psi, N)$-equivariant and also $(\omega_{\pi}, Z)$-equivariant, namely, \begin{align} j_{\pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi} \left ( n(x)z(c) t(a) \varw_0 n(y) \right ) = \psi (x) \psi (y) \omega_{\pi} (c ) j_{\pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi} ( t(a) \varw_0 ). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: $j_{\pi,\psi}$ on the open Bruhat cell: $\boldsymbol J_{\mu,m}(-\lambda^2a)$ on $t(a)\varw_0$, extended by $(\psi,N)$- and $(\omega_\pi,Z)$-equivariance.

nodes.name: eq (4.3) j on torus
nodes.statement: j_{\pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi} ( t(a) \varw_0 ) = \left\{ \begin{split} & |\lambdaup a| \boldsymbol J_{ \mu,\hskip 0.5 pt m} \left ( - \lambdaup^2 a \right ), \hskip 42 pt \text {if } m \text{ is even},\\ & - i |\lambdaup| {\textstyle \sqrt { |a| a}} \boldsymbol J_{ \mu,\hskip 0.5 pt m} \left ( - \lambdaup^2 a \right ), \hskip 5 pt \text {if } m \text{ is odd}, \end{split} \right.
nodes.label: 4eq : j = J

nodes.name: eq (4.4) equivariance of j
nodes.statement: j_{\pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi} \left ( n(x)z(c) t(a) \varw_0 n(y) \right ) = \psi (x) \psi (y) \omega_{\pi} (c ) j_{\pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi} ( t(a) \varw_0 ).
nodes.label: 4eq: psi variant

nodes.name: Kernel formula for the Weyl element action
nodes.statement: W_{\varv} \left ( t (b) \varw_0 \right ) = \int_{{\mathbb {C}}^{\times} } \omega_\pi ( a )\- j ( t(ab) \varw_0) W_{\varv} \left ( t (a) \right ) d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a, \hskip 10 pt \text{ all } \varv \in H_{\infty}.
conclusions: W_{\varv} \left ( t (b) \varw_0 \right ) = \int_{{\mathbb {C}}^{\times} } \omega_\pi ( a )\- j ( t(ab) \varw_0) W_{\varv} \left ( t (a) \right ) d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a, \hskip 10 pt \text{ all } \varv \in H_{\infty}.
nodes.statement_short: The Weyl element acts in the Whittaker/Kirillov model by a Hankel transform with kernel the Bessel function $j$.
nodes.label: 4eq: Weyl element action

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.2
nodes.statement: As an easy consequence of \eqref{4eq: psi variant} and \eqref{4eq: Weyl element action}, we have the following formula.
nodes.statement_short: Combine the kernel formula with the equivariance of $j$.

nodes.name: Whittaker function on the big cell via the Bessel kernel
nodes.statement: Let $\varv \in H_{\infty}$. Then \begin{align} W_{\varv} \left ( g \right ) = \int_{{\mathbb {C}}^{\times} } j \big( g t \big( a\- \big) \big) W_{\varv} \left ( t (a) \right ) d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a, \end{align} for all $ g \in B \varw_0 B$.
conclusions: \begin{align} W_{\varv} \left ( g \right ) = \int_{{\mathbb {C}}^{\times} } j \big( g t \big( a\- \big) \big) W_{\varv} \left ( t (a) \right ) d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a, \end{align} for all $ g \in B \varw_0 B$.
nodes.statement_short: $W_v(g)$ on $B\varw_0B$ is the integral of $j(gt(a^{-1}))W_v(t(a))$ over the torus.
nodes.label: thm: W(g) on BwB

nodes.name: eq (4.6)
nodes.statement: W_{\varv} \left ( g \right ) = \int_{{\mathbb {C}}^{\times} } j \big( g t \big( a\- \big) \big) W_{\varv} \left ( t (a) \right ) d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a,

nodes.name: eq (4.7) j on SL2
nodes.statement: j_{\pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi} ( s (a) \varw ) = (-1)^m \left|\lambdaup a^2 \right| \boldsymbol J_{ \mu,\hskip 0.5 pt m} \left ( \lambdaup^2 a^2 \right ),
nodes.label: 4eq: j = J, SL

nodes.name: eq (4.8) equivariance on SL2
nodes.statement: j_{\pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi} \left ( n(x) s (a) \varw n(y) \right ) = \psi (x) \psi (y) j_{\pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi} ( s (a) \varw ).
nodes.label: 4eq: psi variant, SL

nodes.name: Kernel formula for SL_2(C)
nodes.statement: Of course, the factor $ \omega_\pi ( a )\-$ in \eqref{4eq: Weyl element action} disappears if $\pi $ is a representation of ${\mathrm {PGL}}_2 ({\mathbb {C}})$ in the case when $m$ is even. Otherwise, it will be gone if one uses $s (a)$ instead of $t (a)$ for torus elements, so the kernel formula looks simpler for ${\mathrm {SL}}_2 ({\mathbb {C}})$, \begin{equation} W_{\varv} \left ( s (b) \varw \right ) = \int_{{\mathbb {C}}^{\times} } j ( s(ab) \varw ) W_{\varv} \left ( s (a) \right ) d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a, \end{equation} for all $\varv \in H_{\infty}$. See \cite[Theorem 2]{Mo-Kernel} and \cite[Theorem 2.3]{Baruch-Kernel}.
nodes.statement_short: The $\omega_\pi$ factor disappears for $\mathrm{PGL}_2$ or with $s(a)$, giving the simpler $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{C})$ kernel formula.

nodes.name: eq (4.9)
nodes.statement: W_{\varv} \left ( s (b) \varw \right ) = \int_{{\mathbb {C}}^{\times} } j ( s(ab) \varw ) W_{\varv} \left ( s (a) \right ) d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a,

nodes.name: extension of j by zero
nodes.statement: We extend the definition of $j $ to the whole group $G$ by setting $j (g)=0$ for $g\notin X $.

nodes.name: Local integrability of the Bessel function j
nodes.statement: Assume that $\pi $ is unitary. Then $j $ is locally integrable over $G$. Namely, for any $f\in C_c^\infty(G)$, we have \[ \int_G \left|f(g)j (g) \right| dg<\infty. \]
conclusions: $j $ is locally integrable over $G$.
nodes.label: thm: local integrability

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.4
nodes.statement: Recall that the measure on $X = NA \varw_0 N$ is given by $ d g = |a|^{-2} d x \hskip 1 pt d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a \hskip 1 pt d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt c \hskip 1 pt d y$ if $g = n(x)z(c)t(a)\varw_0n(y)$. We have \begin{align*} \int_G |f(g)j (g)| dg = \ & \int_{X}|f(g)j (g)|dg \\ = \ &\int |j (t(a)\varw_0)|\left(\iiint |f(n(x)z(c)t(a)\varw_0n(y))|dxdyd^{\times} \hskip -1 pt c \right) |a|^{-2}d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a \\ = \ & \int |j (t(a)\varw_0)| \left ( \int J \big( \sqrt a, c, |f| \big) d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt c \right ) |a|^{-2} d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a, \end{align*} where $ J \big( \sqrt a, c, |f| \big) $ is the orbital integral defined as in \eqref{def: J (a,c,f)}. In view of Proposition \ref{prop:A1}, the inner integral over $c$ is zero for small $|a|$ and of the order $|a|^{1+\varepsilon}$ for large $|a|$. In view of Lemma \ref{4lem: bounds for J} and the expression of $j = j_{\pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi}$ as in \eqref{4eq : j = J}, $j (t(a) \varw_0)$ is bounded by $ {|a|}^{\frac 1 2}$ when $|a|$ is large. It is now clear that the integral above is convergent.
nodes.statement_short: Bruhat coordinates reduce to a torus integral; bound the orbital integral by Prop. A.1 and $j$ by Lemma 4.1.

nodes.name: measure on X
nodes.statement: Recall that the measure on $X = NA \varw_0 N$ is given by $ d g = |a|^{-2} d x \hskip 1 pt d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a \hskip 1 pt d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt c \hskip 1 pt d y$ if $g = n(x)z(c)t(a)\varw_0n(y)$.
nodes.statement_short: Recall the Haar measure in Bruhat coordinates.

nodes.name: reduce to orbital integral
nodes.statement: We have \begin{align*} \int_G |f(g)j (g)| dg = \ & \int_{X}|f(g)j (g)|dg \\ = \ &\int |j (t(a)\varw_0)|\left(\iiint |f(n(x)z(c)t(a)\varw_0n(y))|dxdyd^{\times} \hskip -1 pt c \right) |a|^{-2}d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a \\ = \ & \int |j (t(a)\varw_0)| \left ( \int J \big( \sqrt a, c, |f| \big) d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt c \right ) |a|^{-2} d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a, \end{align*} where $ J \big( \sqrt a, c, |f| \big) $ is the orbital integral defined as in \eqref{def: J (a,c,f)}.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite as torus integral of $|j|$ against an orbital integral.

nodes.name: bound orbital integral
nodes.statement: In view of Proposition \ref{prop:A1}, the inner integral over $c$ is zero for small $|a|$ and of the order $|a|^{1+\varepsilon}$ for large $|a|$.
nodes.statement_short: Prop. A.1 bounds the inner orbital integral.

nodes.name: bound j and conclude
nodes.statement: In view of Lemma \ref{4lem: bounds for J} and the expression of $j = j_{\pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi}$ as in \eqref{4eq : j = J}, $j (t(a) \varw_0)$ is bounded by $ {|a|}^{\frac 1 2}$ when $|a|$ is large. It is now clear that the integral above is convergent.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 4.1 bounds $j$; the integral converges.

nodes.name: Torus integral of the Bessel distribution
nodes.statement: {} Let $\varv\in H_\infty$, then \[ \int_{{\mathbb {C}}^{\times}}J(\rho_r(t(a))f)W_{\varv}(t(a))d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a=\int_Gf(g)W_{\varv}(g)dg, \] in which $\rho_r$ is the right translation, that is, $(\rho_r (h) f)(g) = f ( g h)$.
nodes.statement_short: Integrating $J(\rho_r(t(a))f)$ against $W_v(t(a))$ gives $\int_G fW_v$.
nodes.label: le41

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.1
nodes.statement: The proof is similar to that of \cite[Lemma 7.1]{BaruchMao-Real}. For any $\varv\in H_\infty$, we have \begin{align*} \pi(\rho_r(t(a))f) \varv & = \int_G f(gt(a))\pi(g) \varv \hskip 0.5 pt dg \\ & =\int_G f(g)\pi(g)\pi(t(a^{-1})) \varv\hskip 0.5 pt dg = \pi (f) \pi(t(a^{-1})) \varv. \end{align*} Thus it follow from \eqref{def: vector v l f}, \eqref{def: J (f)} and \eqref{def: Wv(g)} that $\varv_{L,\hskip 1 pt \rho_r(t(a))f}=\pi(t(a))\varv_{L, \hskip 0.5 pt f}$ and $J (\rho_r(t(a))f)=\overline {W_{\varv_{L, \hskip 0.5 pt f}}(t(a))}$. Hence, in view of \eqref{eq: inner product}, we have \[ \int_{{\mathbb {C}}^{\times}} J (\rho_r(t(a))f)W_\varv(t(a))d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a=\langle \varv,\varv_{L, \hskip 0.5 pt f} \rangle. \] On the other hand, by \eqref{def: vector v l f} and \eqref{def: Wv(g)}, \[ \langle \varv,\varv_{L, \hskip 0.5 pt f} \rangle =L(\pi(f)\varv)=\int_G f(g)W_\varv(g)dg, \] which finishes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Identify $J(\rho_r(t(a))f)$ with $\overline{W_{v_{L,f}}(t(a))}$ and use the inner product formula (3.1).

nodes.name: as Baruch-Mao
nodes.statement: The proof is similar to that of \cite[Lemma 7.1]{BaruchMao-Real}.
nodes.statement_short: Same as Baruch-Mao Lemma 7.1.

nodes.name: right translation
nodes.statement: For any $\varv\in H_\infty$, we have \begin{align*} \pi(\rho_r(t(a))f) \varv & = \int_G f(gt(a))\pi(g) \varv \hskip 0.5 pt dg \\ & =\int_G f(g)\pi(g)\pi(t(a^{-1})) \varv\hskip 0.5 pt dg = \pi (f) \pi(t(a^{-1})) \varv. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Right translation by $t(a)$ intertwines with $\pi(t(a^{-1}))$.

nodes.name: identify J
nodes.statement: Thus it follow from \eqref{def: vector v l f}, \eqref{def: J (f)} and \eqref{def: Wv(g)} that $\varv_{L,\hskip 1 pt \rho_r(t(a))f}=\pi(t(a))\varv_{L, \hskip 0.5 pt f}$ and $J (\rho_r(t(a))f)=\overline {W_{\varv_{L, \hskip 0.5 pt f}}(t(a))}$.
nodes.statement_short: $J(\rho_r(t(a))f)=\overline{W_{v_{L,f}}(t(a))}$.

nodes.name: inner product
nodes.statement: Hence, in view of \eqref{eq: inner product}, we have \[ \int_{{\mathbb {C}}^{\times}} J (\rho_r(t(a))f)W_\varv(t(a))d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a=\langle \varv,\varv_{L, \hskip 0.5 pt f} \rangle. \]
nodes.statement_short: Inner product formula turns the integral into $\langle v,v_{L,f}\rangle$.

nodes.name: conclude
nodes.statement: On the other hand, by \eqref{def: vector v l f} and \eqref{def: Wv(g)}, \[ \langle \varv,\varv_{L, \hskip 0.5 pt f} \rangle =L(\pi(f)\varv)=\int_G f(g)W_\varv(g)dg, \] which finishes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: $\langle v,v_{L,f}\rangle=\int_G fW_v$.

nodes.name: distribution tilde J
nodes.statement: We define a distribution $\widetilde J = \widetilde J_{\pi,\hskip 0.5 pt \psi}$ on $C_c^\infty(G)$ by \[ \widetilde J (f)=\int_{G}f(g)j(g)dg. \]

nodes.name: Torus integral of the Bessel-function distribution
nodes.statement: {}\footnote{Lemma \ref{le42} is stronger than Lemma 7.2 in \cite{BaruchMao-Real} as our computation shows that it is not necessary to assume that $W_{\varv} (t(a))$ has a high order of vanishing at $a = 0$.} Let $\varv\in H_\infty$ and $f\in C_c^\infty(G)$. Then \[ \int_{{\mathbb {C}}^{\times}} \widetilde J (\rho_r(t(a)) f)W_{\varv}(t(a))d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a=\int_G f(g)W_{\varv}(g)dg. \]
nodes.statement_short: The same torus identity as Lemma 5.1 holds for $\widetilde J$, without vanishing assumptions on $W_v$.
nodes.label: le42

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.2
nodes.statement: We have \begin{align*} & \hskip 13 pt \int \widetilde J (\rho_r(t(a)) f)W_{\varv}(t(a))d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a \\ &= \int \left(\int_{X}f(gt(a))j (g)dg\right) W_\varv(t(a)) d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a \\ &= \int \left( \int_{X}f(g)j (gt(a^{-1}))dg \right) W_\varv(t(a))d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a \\ &= \int_{X} f(g) \left( \int j (gt(a^{-1}))W_\varv(t(a))d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a \right)dg \\ &= \int_{X} f(g)W_\varv(g)dg. \end{align*} Here we have obtained the last equality from \eqref{thm: W(g) on BwB} in Theorem \ref{thm: W(g) on BwB}. It is however needed to justify the change of order of integrations in the second to the last equality. For this, it suffices to verify the absolute convergence of the integral in the third line. Note that \begin{align*} &\int_{X}|f(g)j (gt(a^{-1}))|dg \\ = \ &\int |j (t(ab)\varw_0)|\left(\iiint |f(n(x)z(c)t(b)\varw_0n(y))|dxdyd^{\times} \hskip -1 pt c \right) |b|^{-2}d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt b \\ = \ & \int |j (t(ab)\varw_0)| \left ( \int J \big( \sqrt b, c, |f| \big) d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt c \right ) |b|^{-2} d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt b, \end{align*} where $ J \big( \sqrt b, c, |f| \big) $ is the orbital integral defined as in \eqref{def: J (a,c,f)}. In view of Proposition \ref{prop:A1}, the inner integral over $c$ is dominated by $ |b|^{1 + \varepsilon} \Upsilon_B (b)$ for some constant $B$, with $\Upsilon_B$ the characteristic function on $\{ b: |b| \geqslant B \}$. Since $\pi = \pi_{\mu, \hskip 0.5 pt m}$ is unitary, we have $|{\mathrm{Re}\,} \mu | < \frac 1 2$. In view of Lemma \ref{4lem: bounds for J} and the expression of $j = j_{\pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi}$ as in \eqref{4eq : j = J}, $j (t(a) \varw_0)$ is bounded by $1 + {|a|}^{\frac 1 2}$. Consequently, we have the following estimations for the integral above \begin{align*} \lll \int \big( 1 + {|ab|}^{\frac 1 2} \big) |b|^{- 3 + \varepsilon} \Upsilon_B (b) d b \lll 1 + |a|^{\frac 1 2}. \end{align*} Finally, recall from Lemma \ref{lem: asymptotic of W(t(a))} that $W_{\varv} (t(a))$ is rapidly decreasing at infinity and of the order $|a|^{2\rho}$ near zero for certain $\rho > 0$, then follows the absolute convergence of the integral.
nodes.statement_short: Unfold, swap integrals and apply Theorem 4.2. The swap is justified by bounding orbital integrals (Prop. A.1) and $j$ (Lemma 4.1) and using Lemma 2.1.

nodes.name: apply Theorem 4.2
nodes.statement: We have \begin{align*} & \hskip 13 pt \int \widetilde J (\rho_r(t(a)) f)W_{\varv}(t(a))d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a \\ &= \int \left(\int_{X}f(gt(a))j (g)dg\right) W_\varv(t(a)) d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a \\ &= \int \left( \int_{X}f(g)j (gt(a^{-1}))dg \right) W_\varv(t(a))d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a \\ &= \int_{X} f(g) \left( \int j (gt(a^{-1}))W_\varv(t(a))d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a \right)dg \\ &= \int_{X} f(g)W_\varv(g)dg. \end{align*} Here we have obtained the last equality from \eqref{thm: W(g) on BwB} in Theorem \ref{thm: W(g) on BwB}.
nodes.statement_short: Unfold, interchange integrals and use the kernel formula of Theorem 4.2.

nodes.name: reduce to absolute convergence
nodes.statement: It is however needed to justify the change of order of integrations in the second to the last equality. For this, it suffices to verify the absolute convergence of the integral in the third line.
nodes.statement_short: It suffices to prove absolute convergence.

nodes.name: orbital integral form
nodes.statement: Note that \begin{align*} &\int_{X}|f(g)j (gt(a^{-1}))|dg \\ = \ &\int |j (t(ab)\varw_0)|\left(\iiint |f(n(x)z(c)t(b)\varw_0n(y))|dxdyd^{\times} \hskip -1 pt c \right) |b|^{-2}d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt b \\ = \ & \int |j (t(ab)\varw_0)| \left ( \int J \big( \sqrt b, c, |f| \big) d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt c \right ) |b|^{-2} d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt b, \end{align*} where $ J \big( \sqrt b, c, |f| \big) $ is the orbital integral defined as in \eqref{def: J (a,c,f)}.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite in Bruhat coordinates with the orbital integral.

nodes.name: bound orbital integral
nodes.statement: In view of Proposition \ref{prop:A1}, the inner integral over $c$ is dominated by $ |b|^{1 + \varepsilon} \Upsilon_B (b)$ for some constant $B$, with $\Upsilon_B$ the characteristic function on $\{ b: |b| \geqslant B \}$.
nodes.statement_short: Prop. A.1 bounds the orbital integral.

nodes.name: bound j
nodes.statement: Since $\pi = \pi_{\mu, \hskip 0.5 pt m}$ is unitary, we have $|{\mathrm{Re}\,} \mu | < \frac 1 2$. In view of Lemma \ref{4lem: bounds for J} and the expression of $j = j_{\pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi}$ as in \eqref{4eq : j = J}, $j (t(a) \varw_0)$ is bounded by $1 + {|a|}^{\frac 1 2}$. Consequently, we have the following estimations for the integral above \begin{align*} \lll \int \big( 1 + {|ab|}^{\frac 1 2} \big) |b|^{- 3 + \varepsilon} \Upsilon_B (b) d b \lll 1 + |a|^{\frac 1 2}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 4.1 bounds $j$, giving $\ll 1+|a|^{1/2}$.

nodes.name: conclude
nodes.statement: Finally, recall from Lemma \ref{lem: asymptotic of W(t(a))} that $W_{\varv} (t(a))$ is rapidly decreasing at infinity and of the order $|a|^{2\rho}$ near zero for certain $\rho > 0$, then follows the absolute convergence of the integral.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 2.1 controls $W_v(t(a))$, so the integral converges.

nodes.name: Regularity of the Bessel distribution on GL_2(C)
nodes.statement: {} The two distributions $\widetilde J $ and $J $ are the same. That is, for any $f\in C_c^\infty(G)$, we have \[ J (f)=\int_G f(g)j (g)dg. \]
conclusions: The two distributions $\widetilde J $ and $J $ are the same.
nodes.statement_short: The Bessel distribution $J_{\pi,\psi}$ is represented by the Bessel function $j_{\pi,\psi}$.
nodes.label: cor53

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 5.3
nodes.statement: Choose $\varv\in H_\infty$ with $W_{\varv} (1) = 1$, say. By Lemma \ref{le41} and \ref{le42} we have \[ \int J (\rho_r(t(a))f)W_\varv(t(a))d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a=\int \widetilde J (\rho_r(t(a))f)W_\varv(t(a))d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a \] for all $f\in C_c^\infty(G)$. We replace $\varv$ by $\pi(n)\varv$ for any $n\in N$ and apply Lemma \ref{le21}, it follows that \[ J (\rho_r(t(a))f)W_\varv(t(a))=\widetilde J (\rho_r(t(a))f)W_\varv(t(a)) \] for all $a\in {\mathbb {C}}^{\times}$. Letting $a = 1$, the conclusion follows immediately.
nodes.statement_short: Compare Lemmas 5.1 and 5.2 and apply Lemma 2.2, then set $a=1$.

nodes.name: compare Lemmas 5.1, 5.2
nodes.statement: Choose $\varv\in H_\infty$ with $W_{\varv} (1) = 1$, say. By Lemma \ref{le41} and \ref{le42} we have \[ \int J (\rho_r(t(a))f)W_\varv(t(a))d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a=\int \widetilde J (\rho_r(t(a))f)W_\varv(t(a))d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a \] for all $f\in C_c^\infty(G)$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemmas 5.1 and 5.2 give equal torus integrals.

nodes.name: apply Lemma 2.2 and conclude
nodes.statement: We replace $\varv$ by $\pi(n)\varv$ for any $n\in N$ and apply Lemma \ref{le21}, it follows that \[ J (\rho_r(t(a))f)W_\varv(t(a))=\widetilde J (\rho_r(t(a))f)W_\varv(t(a)) \] for all $a\in {\mathbb {C}}^{\times}$. Letting $a = 1$, the conclusion follows immediately.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 2.2 gives pointwise equality; set $a=1$.

nodes.name: sigma and pi unitary principal series
nodes.statement: Let $\sigma=\sigma_{\mu, \hskip 0.5 pt m}$ and $\pi=\pi_{\mu, \hskip 0.5 pt m}$ be unitary principal series of $S$ and $G$ respectively; see \S \ref{sec: representations of G and S}.

nodes.name: Regularity of the Bessel distribution on SL_2(C)
nodes.statement: Let $\sigma $ and $\pi$ be as above. For any $h\in C_c^\infty(S)$, we have \[ J_{\sigma,\hskip 0.5 pt \psi}(h)=\int_S h(s) j_{\pi,\hskip 0.5 pt \psi}(s) ds. \] As such, we shall write $j_{\sigma, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi} $ the restriction of $j_{\pi,\hskip 0.5 pt \psi}$ on $S$.
conclusions: we have \[ J_{\sigma,\hskip 0.5 pt \psi}(h)=\int_S h(s) j_{\pi,\hskip 0.5 pt \psi}(s) ds. \]
nodes.statement_short: $J_{\sigma,\psi}$ is represented by the restriction of $j_{\pi,\psi}$ to $S$.
nodes.label: prop54: regularity of J on S

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.4
nodes.statement: Fix $h\in C_c^\infty(S)$. Let $U \subset Z$ be a small open neighborhood of the identity $1$ so that the map $ (s, z) \rightarrow s z $ is an injection from $S \times U$ into $G = S \cdot Z$. Choose a function $\textit{w} \in C_c^{\infty} (U)$ with \begin{align*} \int_{U} \textit{w}(z) d z = 1, \end{align*} where $d z = d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt c$ if $z = z(c)$. Set $f (s z) = h (s) \omega_{\pi}\- (z) \textit{w} (z) $. Clearly, $f$ is well defined and $f \in C_c^{\infty} (G)$ (indeed, $f \in C_c^{\infty} (S \cdot U)$). By Corollary \ref{cor53}, along with the $(\omega_{\pi}, Z)$-equivariance of $j_{\pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi}$ (see \eqref{4eq: psi variant}), we have \begin{align*} J_{\pi,\hskip 0.5 pt \psi}( f)&=\int_G f(g) j_{\pi,\hskip 0.5 pt \psi}(g) dg = \int_{U} \textit{w}(z)d z \int_Sh(s) j_{\pi,\hskip 0.5 pt \psi}(s)ds = \int_S h(s) j_{\pi,\hskip 0.5 pt \psi}(s)ds. \end{align*} On the other hand, since $\sigma$ is the restriction of $\pi$ to $S$, we may prove in a similar fashion that $\pi (f) \varv = \sigma (h) \varv$ for any $\varv \in H$. Precisely, \begin{align*} \int_G f(g)\pi(g)\varv \, dg = \int_{U } \textit{w}(z)d z \int_S h(s) \pi(s)\varv \, ds = \int_S h(s) \sigma (s)\varv \, ds. \end{align*} In view of the definitions in \S \ref{sec: distributions}, it follows that $\varv_{L, \hskip 0.5 pt f}=\varv_{L,\hskip 0.5 pt h}$ and that $J_{\pi,\hskip 0.5 pt \psi}(f)=J_{\sigma,\hskip 0.5 pt \psi}(h)$. The proof is now completed.
nodes.statement_short: Extend $h$ on $S$ to $f$ on $G=S\cdot Z$ with a bump function on $Z$ and apply Corollary 5.3.

nodes.name: choose U and bump w
nodes.statement: Fix $h\in C_c^\infty(S)$. Let $U \subset Z$ be a small open neighborhood of the identity $1$ so that the map $ (s, z) \rightarrow s z $ is an injection from $S \times U$ into $G = S \cdot Z$. Choose a function $\textit{w} \in C_c^{\infty} (U)$ with \begin{align*} \int_{U} \textit{w}(z) d z = 1, \end{align*} where $d z = d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt c$ if $z = z(c)$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix $h$, a neighbourhood $U\subset Z$ and a bump $w$ with integral 1.

nodes.name: construct f
nodes.statement: Set $f (s z) = h (s) \omega_{\pi}\- (z) \textit{w} (z) $. Clearly, $f$ is well defined and $f \in C_c^{\infty} (G)$ (indeed, $f \in C_c^{\infty} (S \cdot U)$).
nodes.statement_short: Define $f(sz)=h(s)\omega_\pi^{-1}(z)w(z)\in C_c^\infty(G)$.

nodes.name: apply Corollary 5.3
nodes.statement: By Corollary \ref{cor53}, along with the $(\omega_{\pi}, Z)$-equivariance of $j_{\pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi}$ (see \eqref{4eq: psi variant}), we have \begin{align*} J_{\pi,\hskip 0.5 pt \psi}( f)&=\int_G f(g) j_{\pi,\hskip 0.5 pt \psi}(g) dg = \int_{U} \textit{w}(z)d z \int_Sh(s) j_{\pi,\hskip 0.5 pt \psi}(s)ds = \int_S h(s) j_{\pi,\hskip 0.5 pt \psi}(s)ds. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Corollary 5.3 and $Z$-equivariance give $J_\pi(f)=\int_S hj$.

nodes.name: pi(f)=sigma(h)
nodes.statement: On the other hand, since $\sigma$ is the restriction of $\pi$ to $S$, we may prove in a similar fashion that $\pi (f) \varv = \sigma (h) \varv$ for any $\varv \in H$. Precisely, \begin{align*} \int_G f(g)\pi(g)\varv \, dg = \int_{U } \textit{w}(z)d z \int_S h(s) \pi(s)\varv \, ds = \int_S h(s) \sigma (s)\varv \, ds. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: $\pi(f)v=\sigma(h)v$.

nodes.name: conclude
nodes.statement: In view of the definitions in \S \ref{sec: distributions}, it follows that $\varv_{L, \hskip 0.5 pt f}=\varv_{L,\hskip 0.5 pt h}$ and that $J_{\pi,\hskip 0.5 pt \psi}(f)=J_{\sigma,\hskip 0.5 pt \psi}(h)$. The proof is now completed.
nodes.statement_short: Hence $J_\pi(f)=J_\sigma(h)$.

nodes.name: (N,N) orbital integral on S
nodes.statement: For $h \in C_c^{\infty} (S)$ we introduced the orbital integral \begin{align} O^{N, \hskip 0.5 pt N}_{h, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi} (g) = \iint h (n(x) g n(y) ) \psi (x) \psi (y) d x d y. \end{align}

nodes.name: eq (5.1) O^{N,N}
nodes.statement: O^{N, \hskip 0.5 pt N}_{h, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi} (g) = \iint h (n(x) g n(y) ) \psi (x) \psi (y) d x d y.
nodes.label: eq: O NN (g)

nodes.name: Jacquet: convergence of (N,N) orbital integrals
nodes.statement: In particular, it is proven in \cite{Jacquet-RTF} that the integral in \eqref{eq: O NN (g)} converges absolutely for all $g \in X \cap S = N (A\cap S) \varw N$.
conclusions: the integral in \eqref{eq: O NN (g)} converges absolutely for all $g \in X \cap S = N (A\cap S) \varw N$

nodes.name: eq (5.2) J_sigma via orbital integral
nodes.statement: J_{\sigma,\hskip 0.5 pt \psi} (h) = \int O^{N, \hskip 0.5 pt N}_{h, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi} (s(a) \varw) j_{\sigma,\hskip 0.5 pt \psi} (s(a) \varw) \|a\|^{-2} d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a.
nodes.label: eq: J = int O

nodes.name: Fourier transform (Lebesgue form)
nodes.statement: The Fourier transform $\widehat f $ of a Schwartz function $f$ on ${\mathbb {C}}$ is defined by \begin{equation*} \widehat f (u) = \sideset{ }{_{\mathbb {C}} }{\iint} \hskip 0.5 pt f (z) e(- {\mathrm{Tr}} (uz) ) \hskip 0.5 pt i d z \hskip - 2 pt \wedge \hskip - 2 pt d \overline z. \end{equation*}
nodes.section: 6.1 A formula for the Fourier transform of Bessel functions

nodes.name: Distributional Fourier transform formula for Bessel functions
nodes.statement: \begin{split} \sideset{ }{_{{\mathbb {C}} } }{\iint} \hskip - 2 pt \boldsymbol J_{\mu,\hskip 0.5 pt m} \left ( z \right ) \widehat f (z) \frac {i d z \hskip - 2 pt \wedge \hskip - 2 pt d \overline z} { {|z|}} = \frac 1 2 \sideset{ }{_{{\mathbb {C}} } }{\iint} e \left ( {\mathrm{Tr}} \left ( \frac 1 {2 u} \right ) \right ) \hskip - 2 pt \boldsymbol J_{\frac 1 2 \mu,\hskip 0.5 pt \frac 1 2 m} \left ( \frac 1 { 16 u ^{ 2} } \right ) \hskip - 1 pt f (u) \frac {i d u \hskip - 2 pt \wedge \hskip - 2 pt d \overline u} { {|u|}}, \end{split}
nodes.section: 6.1 A formula for the Fourier transform of Bessel functions
conclusions: \begin{split} \sideset{ }{_{{\mathbb {C}} } }{\iint} \hskip - 2 pt \boldsymbol J_{\mu,\hskip 0.5 pt m} \left ( z \right ) \widehat f (z) \frac {i d z \hskip - 2 pt \wedge \hskip - 2 pt d \overline z} { {|z|}} = \frac 1 2 \sideset{ }{_{{\mathbb {C}} } }{\iint} e \left ( {\mathrm{Tr}} \left ( \frac 1 {2 u} \right ) \right ) \hskip - 2 pt \boldsymbol J_{\frac 1 2 \mu,\hskip 0.5 pt \frac 1 2 m} \left ( \frac 1 { 16 u ^{ 2} } \right ) \hskip - 1 pt f (u) \frac {i d u \hskip - 2 pt \wedge \hskip - 2 pt d \overline u} { {|u|}}, \end{split}
nodes.statement_short: Distributional form of the complex Weber-Hardy formula: pairing $\boldsymbol J_{\mu,m}$ with $\hat f$ equals pairing $e(\mathrm{Tr}(1/2u))\boldsymbol J_{\mu/2,m/2}(1/16u^2)$ with $f$.
nodes.label: 6eq: Fourier

nodes.name: eq (6.2) Fourier transform of j
nodes.statement: \sideset{ }{_{{\mathbb {C}}^{\times}} }{\int} j_{\pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi} ( t(a) \varw_0 ) \widehat f (a) d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a = \sideset{ }{_{{\mathbb {C}}^{\times}} }{\int} e \left ( {\mathrm{Tr}} ({\lambdaup} / {2 x} ) \right ) \left| \lambdaup / 2 x \right| \boldsymbol J_{\frac 1 2 \mu,\hskip 0.5 pt \frac 1 2 m} \left ( \lambdaup^2 / 16 x^2 \right ) f (x ) { d x } ,
nodes.section: 6.1 A formula for the Fourier transform of Bessel functions
nodes.label: 6eq: Fourier transform of j

nodes.name: pi with trivial central character
nodes.statement: Let $\pi$ be an infinite-dimensional irreducible unitary representation of $G = {\mathrm {GL}}_2 ({\mathbb {C}})$ with trivial central character.

nodes.name: eq (6.3) I on X
nodes.statement: I (f) = \frac 1 {L (\pi, 1/2)} \int_{{\mathbb {C}}^{\times}} \left ( \int_{X} f(t(b)g) j (g) dg \right ) d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt b .
nodes.label: 6eq: I = int

nodes.name: Relative Bessel distribution on split test functions
nodes.statement: Let $f \in C_c^{\infty} (X)$ be of the form \begin{align} f (t(a) z(c) n(x) \varw_0 n(y)) = f_1 (a) f_2 (c) f_3 (x) f_4 (y), \end{align} with $f_1, f_2 \in C_c^{\infty} ({\mathbb {C}}^{\times})$ and $f_3, f_4 \in C_c^{\infty} ({\mathbb {C}})$. Then \begin{equation} \begin{split} & \int_{{\mathbb {C}}^{\times}} \int_{G} f(t(b)g) j (g) dg \hskip 0.5 pt d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt b \\ = \ & \int_{{\mathbb {C}}^{\times}} f_1 (b) d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt b \int_{{\mathbb {C}}^{\times}} f_2 (c) d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt c \int_{{\mathbb {C}}} f_4 (y ) \psi (y) d y \int_{{\mathbb {C}}^{\times}} j (t(a) \varw_0) \widehat f_3 (a) d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a, \end{split} \end{equation} where $ \widehat f_2 $ is the $\psi$-Fourier transform of $f_2$ defined as in \eqref{def: Fourier}.
assumptions: Let $f \in C_c^{\infty} (X)$ be of the form
with $f_1, f_2 \in C_c^{\infty} ({\mathbb {C}}^{\times})$ and $f_3, f_4 \in C_c^{\infty} ({\mathbb {C}})$
nodes.statement_short: For split $f=f_1f_2f_3f_4$ the double integral factors, leaving $\int j(t(a)\varw_0)\hat f_3(a)d^\times a$.
nodes.label: 6lem: rel Bessel for split f

nodes.name: eq (6.4) split f
nodes.statement: f (t(a) z(c) n(x) \varw_0 n(y)) = f_1 (a) f_2 (c) f_3 (x) f_4 (y),
nodes.label: 6eq: f splits

nodes.name: eq (6.5) double integral
nodes.statement: \begin{split} & \int_{{\mathbb {C}}^{\times}} \int_{G} f(t(b)g) j (g) dg \hskip 0.5 pt d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt b \\ = \ & \int_{{\mathbb {C}}^{\times}} f_1 (b) d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt b \int_{{\mathbb {C}}^{\times}} f_2 (c) d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt c \int_{{\mathbb {C}}} f_4 (y ) \psi (y) d y \int_{{\mathbb {C}}^{\times}} j (t(a) \varw_0) \widehat f_3 (a) d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a, \end{split}
nodes.label: 6eq: double int for I

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6.1
nodes.statement: Let $dg = d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a \hskip 1 pt d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt c \hskip 1 pt d x \hskip 1 pt d y$ be a Haar measure on $X$ for $g = t(a) z(c) n(x) \varw_0 n(y)$. In view of \eqref{4eq: psi variant} and \eqref{6eq: f splits}, the integral on the left hand side of \eqref{6eq: double int for I} splits into the product \begin{align*} & \int f_2 (c) d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt c \int f_4 (y ) \psi (y) d y \int \left ( \int f_1 (ab) j (t(a) \varw_0) \int f_3 (x) \psi ( a x) d x \hskip 0.5 pt d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a \right ) d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt b \\ = \ & \int f_2 (c) d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt c \int f_4 (y ) \psi (y) d y \iint f_1 (ab) j (t(a) \varw_0) \widehat f_3 (a) d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a \hskip 0.5 pt d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt b. \end{align*} We claim that the last double integral converges absolutely. Hence we may change the order of integrations and the variable $b$ to $b/a$, getting \begin{align*} \iint f_1 (ab) j (t(a) \varw_0) \widehat f_3 (a) d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a \hskip 0.5 pt d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt b & = \int j (t(a) \varw_0) \widehat f_3 (a) \int f_1 (ab) d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt b \hskip 0.5 pt d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a \\ & = \int f_1 (b ) d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt b \int j (t(a) \varw_0) \widehat f_3 (a) d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a. \end{align*} We now show the absolute convergence. Choose $|{\mathrm{Re}\,} \mu | < \rho < \frac 1 2$. Lemma \ref{4lem: bounds for J} implies that $j (t(a) \varw_0)$ may be bounded by $|a|^{1 - 2\rho} + {|a|}^{\frac 1 2}$. We can find positive constants $A$ and $B$ such that $f_1 (a ) \lll \Upsilon_{A, B} (a)$, with $ \Upsilon_{A, B} (a)$ defined to be the characteristic function on the annulus $\left\{ a : A \leqslant |a| \leqslant B \right\}$. Hence \begin{align*} \int \big| f_1 (ab) j (t(a) \varw_0) \widehat f_3(a) \big| d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a \lll \int \Upsilon_{A/|b|, B/|b|} (a) \big|\widehat f_3 (a) \big| \big( |a|^{- 1- 2 \rho} + |a|^{- \frac 3 2} \big) d a. \end{align*} Since $\widehat f_3 (a)$ is rapidly decreasing when $|a|$ is large, it follows that the value of the integral above is rapidly decreasing when $|b|$ is small. When $|b|$ is large the integral is bounded by $ |b|^{2 \rho - 1} + |b|^{- \frac 1 2}$. It is then clear that integrating further with $d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt b = d b / |b|^2$ will converge absolutely at both $0$ and $\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Split the integral by equivariance and Fubini after a change of variables. Absolute convergence uses Lemma 4.1 and rapid decay of $\hat f_3$.

nodes.name: split into product
nodes.statement: Let $dg = d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a \hskip 1 pt d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt c \hskip 1 pt d x \hskip 1 pt d y$ be a Haar measure on $X$ for $g = t(a) z(c) n(x) \varw_0 n(y)$. In view of \eqref{4eq: psi variant} and \eqref{6eq: f splits}, the integral on the left hand side of \eqref{6eq: double int for I} splits into the product \begin{align*} & \int f_2 (c) d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt c \int f_4 (y ) \psi (y) d y \int \left ( \int f_1 (ab) j (t(a) \varw_0) \int f_3 (x) \psi ( a x) d x \hskip 0.5 pt d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a \right ) d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt b \\ = \ & \int f_2 (c) d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt c \int f_4 (y ) \psi (y) d y \iint f_1 (ab) j (t(a) \varw_0) \widehat f_3 (a) d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a \hskip 0.5 pt d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt b. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Bruhat coordinates and equivariance split the integral.

nodes.name: claim absolute convergence
nodes.statement: We claim that the last double integral converges absolutely. Hence we may change the order of integrations and the variable $b$ to $b/a$, getting \begin{align*} \iint f_1 (ab) j (t(a) \varw_0) \widehat f_3 (a) d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a \hskip 0.5 pt d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt b & = \int j (t(a) \varw_0) \widehat f_3 (a) \int f_1 (ab) d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt b \hskip 0.5 pt d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a \\ & = \int f_1 (b ) d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt b \int j (t(a) \varw_0) \widehat f_3 (a) d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a. \end{align*} We now show the absolute convergence. Choose $|{\mathrm{Re}\,} \mu | < \rho < \frac 1 2$. Lemma \ref{4lem: bounds for J} implies that $j (t(a) \varw_0)$ may be bounded by $|a|^{1 - 2\rho} + {|a|}^{\frac 1 2}$. We can find positive constants $A$ and $B$ such that $f_1 (a ) \lll \Upsilon_{A, B} (a)$, with $ \Upsilon_{A, B} (a)$ defined to be the characteristic function on the annulus $\left\{ a : A \leqslant |a| \leqslant B \right\}$. Hence \begin{align*} \int \big| f_1 (ab) j (t(a) \varw_0) \widehat f_3(a) \big| d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a \lll \int \Upsilon_{A/|b|, B/|b|} (a) \big|\widehat f_3 (a) \big| \big( |a|^{- 1- 2 \rho} + |a|^{- \frac 3 2} \big) d a. \end{align*} Since $\widehat f_3 (a)$ is rapidly decreasing when $|a|$ is large, it follows that the value of the integral above is rapidly decreasing when $|b|$ is small. When $|b|$ is large the integral is bounded by $ |b|^{2 \rho - 1} + |b|^{- \frac 1 2}$. It is then clear that integrating further with $d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt b = d b / |b|^2$ will converge absolutely at both $0$ and $\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Claim absolute convergence, change variables, and prove the claim.

nodes.name: change order
nodes.statement: Hence we may change the order of integrations and the variable $b$ to $b/a$, getting \begin{align*} \iint f_1 (ab) j (t(a) \varw_0) \widehat f_3 (a) d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a \hskip 0.5 pt d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt b & = \int j (t(a) \varw_0) \widehat f_3 (a) \int f_1 (ab) d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt b \hskip 0.5 pt d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a \\ & = \int f_1 (b ) d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt b \int j (t(a) \varw_0) \widehat f_3 (a) d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Swap integrals and substitute $b\to b/a$.

nodes.name: bound j
nodes.statement: We now show the absolute convergence. Choose $|{\mathrm{Re}\,} \mu | < \rho < \frac 1 2$. Lemma \ref{4lem: bounds for J} implies that $j (t(a) \varw_0)$ may be bounded by $|a|^{1 - 2\rho} + {|a|}^{\frac 1 2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 4.1 bounds $j(t(a)\varw_0)$.

nodes.name: bound f_1
nodes.statement: We can find positive constants $A$ and $B$ such that $f_1 (a ) \lll \Upsilon_{A, B} (a)$, with $ \Upsilon_{A, B} (a)$ defined to be the characteristic function on the annulus $\left\{ a : A \leqslant |a| \leqslant B \right\}$. Hence \begin{align*} \int \big| f_1 (ab) j (t(a) \varw_0) \widehat f_3(a) \big| d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt a \lll \int \Upsilon_{A/|b|, B/|b|} (a) \big|\widehat f_3 (a) \big| \big( |a|^{- 1- 2 \rho} + |a|^{- \frac 3 2} \big) d a. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Bound $f_1$ by an annulus indicator.

nodes.name: conclude convergence
nodes.statement: Since $\widehat f_3 (a)$ is rapidly decreasing when $|a|$ is large, it follows that the value of the integral above is rapidly decreasing when $|b|$ is small. When $|b|$ is large the integral is bounded by $ |b|^{2 \rho - 1} + |b|^{- \frac 1 2}$. It is then clear that integrating further with $d^{\times} \hskip -1 pt b = d b / |b|^2$ will converge absolutely at both $0$ and $\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Rapid decay of $\hat f_3$ gives convergence at $0$ and $\infty$.

nodes.name: Relative Bessel function i_{pi,psi} (definition and representation of I)
nodes.statement: Combining \eqref{6eq: Fourier transform of j}, \eqref{6eq: I = int} and \eqref{6eq: double int for I}, it follows that if we define a function $i = i_{\pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi}$ supported on $U$ such that \begin{align} i_{\pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi} ( n(x) \varw_0 ) = e \left ( {\mathrm{Tr}} ({\lambdaup} / {2 x} ) \right ) \left| \lambdaup / 2 x \right| \boldsymbol J_{\frac 1 2 \mu,\hskip 0.5 pt \frac 1 2 m} \left ( \lambdaup^2 / 16 x^2 \right ) / {L (\pi, 1/2)}, \end{align} and that $i_{\pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi}$ is right $ (\psi, N)$-equivariant and left $A$-invariant, namely, \begin{align} i_{\pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi} (t(a) z(c) n(x) \varw_0 n(y)) = \psi (y) i_{\pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi} ( n(x) \varw_0 ), \end{align} then \begin{align} I_{\pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi} (f) = \int_{U} f (g) i_{\pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi} (g) d g, \end{align} for all $f $ of the form \eqref{6eq: f splits} in Lemma \ref{6lem: rel Bessel for split f}.
conclusions: I_{\pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi} (f) = \int_{U} f (g) i_{\pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi} (g) d g,
nodes.statement_short: Defining $i_{\pi,\psi}$ via $\boldsymbol J_{\mu/2,m/2}(\lambda^2/16x^2)$, the relative Bessel distribution is integration against $i$ for split $f$.

nodes.name: eq (6.6) i on n(x)w0
nodes.statement: i_{\pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi} ( n(x) \varw_0 ) = e \left ( {\mathrm{Tr}} ({\lambdaup} / {2 x} ) \right ) \left| \lambdaup / 2 x \right| \boldsymbol J_{\frac 1 2 \mu,\hskip 0.5 pt \frac 1 2 m} \left ( \lambdaup^2 / 16 x^2 \right ) / {L (\pi, 1/2)},
nodes.label: 6eq: defn of i

nodes.name: eq (6.7) equivariance of i
nodes.statement: i_{\pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi} (t(a) z(c) n(x) \varw_0 n(y)) = \psi (y) i_{\pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi} ( n(x) \varw_0 ),
nodes.label: eq: equivariance of i

nodes.name: eq (6.8) I via i
nodes.statement: I_{\pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi} (f) = \int_{U} f (g) i_{\pi, \hskip 0.5 pt \psi} (g) d g,
nodes.label: 6eq: I = int of i

nodes.name: Regularity of the relative Bessel distribution on the open Bruhat cell
nodes.statement: Since such functions span a dense subspace of $ C_c^{\infty} (X)$ (the Stone-Weierstra\ss \hskip 2.5 pt theorem), \eqref{6eq: I = int of i} is actually valid for all $f \in C_c^{\infty} (X)$.
conclusions: \eqref{6eq: I = int of i} is actually valid for all $f \in C_c^{\infty} (X)$

nodes.name: Local integrability of the relative Bessel function i
nodes.statement: The relative Bessel function $i $ is local integrable on $G$, namely, for any $f\in C_c^\infty(G)$, \[ \int_G |f(g) i (g)|dg< \infty. \]
nodes.section: 7 Regularity of relative Bessel distributions over ${\mathrm {GL}}_2 ({\mathbb {C}})$
conclusions: $i $ is local integrable on $G$
nodes.label: prop81: local integ. of i

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 7.1
nodes.statement: The proof is similar to that of Proposition \ref{thm: local integrability}. nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 7.2
nodes.statement: Let $T$ be the distribution on $G$ defined by the difference $T=I-\widetilde I$. First, in view of \eqref{6eq: I = int of i}, $I$ and $\widetilde I$ coincide on $X$, so $T$ is supported on the Borel $B = G\smallsetminus X$. Second, it is clear that $T$ satisfies $\rho_r(n(y))I=\psi(y)I$. Third, we claim that $T$ is an eigen-distribution of the Casimir element $\varDelta$ in the universal enveloping algebra of the Lie algebra of $G$. To see this, we first note that $I$ is an eigen-distribution of $\varDelta$ according to \cite[\S 3]{Shalika-MO}, that is, $\varDelta I= \kappa I$ ($\kappa \in {\mathbb {C}}$). As aforementioned, $I$ is represented by the (real analytic) function $i$ when restricted on $ U $, so $i$ is an eigen-function of $\varDelta$ on $U$. Precisely, we have $\varDelta \hskip 0.5 pt i = \kappa \hskip 0.5 pt i$, which further implies $\varDelta \widetilde I= \kappa \widetilde I$. The third claim is now proven. Under the three conditions above, by \cite[Proposition 2.10]{Shalika-MO}, we must have $T=0$.
